near_miss.lead: Cognate father/mother/brother/sister terms in kinship enumerations.
near_miss.why_not: Norse inheritance priorities, Russian famine-induced failure of family solidarity, and Sanskrit family attachment or divine genealogy do not share a distinctive syntactic figure or ordered formula. A Rigvedic search for mother/father/brother co-occurrence found varied contexts (RV 1.191.6, 5.34.4, 8.1.6, 10.34.4), reinforcing the low specificity of the kinship list.

near_miss.lead: A woman in the household or authority of mother, father, and brother.
near_miss.why_not: AVŚ 1.14 binds a woman to her natal household; Norse law regulates marriage guardians and inheritance after intercourse in the parental household. The three kinship nouns are cognate, but order and construction vary; garðr and gṛha cannot simply be treated as an exact cognate equation. RV 10.85.24, 26, 46 gives related wedding language without the proposed natal-household triad. Social organization explains the overlap without requiring inherited wording.

near_miss.lead: Eyes as celestial lights; head as sky.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse poetic explanation explicitly identifies the head as sky and eyes as its heavenly bodies. Lucretius 1.64 instead has personified religio showing its head from heaven; Cato 126.1 is a medical wine recipe. Neither slab partner realizes the same figure. The wider solar-eye comparison is reported separately as a search lead.

near_miss.lead: Norse fe and Latin pecus / Vedic paśu in property and protection language.
near_miss.why_not: The cognate cattle/wealth nouns have different local syntactic partners: Norse taxation or forfeiture, Roman livestock as security, and Vedic ritual favor. Repeated fe oc friði is a Norse legal alliteration, not reproduced by the Vedic priyam dhāma wording; shared roots alone do not establish a phrase.

near_miss.lead: Birth as coming alive into light.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse clause is a genuine birth expression; its assigned Sanskrit partners describe mind, worlds attained by filial duty, or reported speech, not entry into light at birth. A Latin parallel found outside the slab is reported separately.

near_miss.lead: Sun in the east and dawn as a time for human activity.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse assembly timetable and AVŚ 18.1 dawn stanza concern different acts and contain no shared marked construction. Ordinary astronomical time reference is insufficient.

near_miss.lead: Lifetime/perpetuity expressed by aldr and æfi.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse legal durability formula has no equivalent temporal binomial in MBh 13.6.s93, which contrasts human and divine worlds and discusses prosperity. A cognate life-root in a compound is insufficient to reconstruct the Norse paired wording.

near_miss.lead: Killing father, mother, and sister/brother as a catalogue of grave wrongs.
near_miss.why_not: Norse drepr governs a kin list; AVP 19.46.s26 has agent compounds mātṛ-hā, pitṛ-hā, svasṛ-hā. Kin terms are cognate but the Norse killing verb is renewed, the enumeration differs, and neither a distinctive syntactic match nor non-generic sequence is secure. RV 5.34.4, found in the kinship search, describes Indra killing a worshipper’s relatives, not the same legal offence. No inherited phrase claimed.

near_miss.lead: Return of a loan safe home; divine arrival from heaven.
near_miss.why_not: Norse hæilu hæim koma is a marked local alliterative collocation, but Catullus 64.299 aduenit caelo has neither safe return nor home as destination. A generic motion predicate does not establish the formula.

near_miss.lead: Law of God and men versus Vedic divine/human ritual language.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse wording is explicitly Christian, including Saint Olaf or Christian marriage law; the Vedic passages lack the corresponding law-merism. Neither shared syntax nor a route excluding Christian development is demonstrated.

search_lead.cognate: Norse líos (lemma ljós/liós) and Latin luminis (lumen) continue light vocabulary from *leuk-. Norse kǫmr is koma, present 3sg; no cognate motion verb is asserted for profudit/edant.
search_lead.argument: Norse kǫmr lífí j líos describes a child emerging alive at birth as a condition of inheritance. Latin likewise places birth or the production of living offspring into the region of light. Both have directional into + light and a birth context. The shared figure is worth reviewing, but Latin adds a shore metaphor and uses causative emergence verbs. Medieval Christian legal transmission and independent development remain possible; this is a search lead, not an established inherited formula.

search_lead.cognate: Norse sol (sól) and Vedic sū́ryaḥ are inherited solar words. No cognacy of auga with cákṣus is asserted.
search_lead.argument: The Norse context before the anchored passage permits calling the eye a sun, while the following poetic example calls eyes heavenly bodies of the head-sky. RV 10.90 derives the sun from the cosmic person’s eye; RV 1.115 calls the rising solar manifestation the eye of gods. These support a comparative eye/sun figure carried by cognate solar vocabulary, but the direction of the image and syntax differ. The Norse list of many possible eye kennings and late attestation limit the inference of a particular inherited phrase.

error.correct_reading: brá, eyelash/eyelid, genitive plural here; not the verb bregða.
error.evidence: The instruction kenna til governs a series of eye-surrounding parts: brá, brúna, hvarma, ennís. A verbal analysis cannot occupy this nominal list.

error.correct_reading: brún, eyebrow, genitive plural brúna; not bruni, burning.
error.evidence: It occurs with eyelids, eyelash/eyelid rims, and forehead in instructions for forming eye kennings.

given_etymon.gloss: to call; to chant; to shout

error.correct_reading: gler, glass: remove the mapping to the calling/chanting root *gʰel-. No precise replacement etymon asserted here.
error.evidence: The list gives bright or reflective objects as eye designations, including glass and gemstones. The supplied calling gloss is not an etymological analysis supported by this noun.

error.correct_reading: Einarr, personal name, nominative singular; mark as name.
error.evidence: qvað introduces a named poet, Einarr Skúlason. The current unknown lemma misses the proper name.

error.correct_reading: Skúlason, patronymic of Einarr; mark as name.
error.evidence: It follows Eínar after qvað and identifies the poet; it is not an unknown common noun.
